title: Ask HN: Is the Microsoft buyout just a long overdue correction?
summary:
I was looking at the head counts recently for Microsoft and comparing with past years.

In 2018 their headcount was around 131,000 employees. In 2020, that jumped to 163,000. By 2022, they had exploded to 221,000 employees.

Currently, if we exclude the Activision headcount, they're sitting at around 218,000 people.

Maybe the more business minded people can shed some light on this for me, but even with the stronger economy in 2018, Microsoft had no where near this many employees. It feels like this would have happened whether or not the economy was doing poorly right now.

Thoughts?

title: Trouble finding a motivated co-founder
summary:
For context, I'm a college student running a consumer mobile app business. I've been working on my own apps solo for about 6 months (both development and marketing), and since I'm majoring in engineering, it's been quite hard to balance running this business with my studies.

This is what originally led me to seek a co-founder in the consumer mobile app space who's strong in UGC/distribution. The problem is that It's very hard for me to find someone who actually cares and is willing to put in the work.

Some past scenarios:

1) I made a profile on the YC Co-founder matching site and got matched with a guy who eventually ghosted me after two weeks. I got matched with a couple of other people as well, but they never answered any of my introduction DMs

2) I met another guy on this one app called "Ambitious" who seemed pretty motivated (he was also a student) and was also interested in mobile apps. But after creating literally 1 single video, he said that he didn't have the time for this and left.

I've tried talking to other students at my university as well, but I don't really go to a prestigious school or one that's known for cs/tech, so not many people are interested in startups or stuff like that.

I'm not quite sure what I should do at this point, so I wanted to come on here and ask for tips and advice for finding a co-founder.

summary:

Subject: Notice of Security Incident

This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.

Hello,

We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.

We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).

We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.

Watch for phishing

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.
For more information

We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.

The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.
We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.

Scribd, Inc.

title: GEMM Tutorial and UlmBLAS
summary:
In 2014 I wrote a tutorial on how to write an efficient matrix multiplication that can achieve near peak performance. This is actually not achieved by some Strassen algorithm variant. It's achieved through a cache friendly algorithm (exploiting the cache hierarchy) and SIMD register instructions.

The tutorial showed how to achieve that step by step. Beginning with a naive implementation using three loops. Then using buffers to first cache matrix blocks and then performing the matrix product block wise. That actually means you make copies of blocks and then do computations with the blocks. Sounds stupid but makes sense: Assume you have square N x N blocks then cost of make making a copy is O(N^2) and for the computation it's O(N^3). If the computation with the copied/cached blocks is much faster this actually pays of.

Anyway the details are explained in the tutorial. As the university web server has changed many times after 2014 I moved it to GitHub: https://github.com/michael-lehn/gemm-tutorial

From the tutorial I created ulmBLAS (ulm makes sense, as I work at Ulm University) which is a complete BLAS implementation. Recently I started with a tutorial for the matrix multiplication with Cuda. Currently there is not much text, I just outlined a possible step by step approach to go from naive to a performant implementation (actually the goal was to be on par with NVIDIA's cuBLAS; but it's more on parish ... but I think still gives an idea). It in the cuda subdirectory of ulmBLAS: https://github.com/michael-lehn/ulmBLAS

title: "Wrong" Email
summary:
Let’s say your LinkedIn account has been restricted, and you can no longer access it. You might try to visit:

https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/sdsupport or https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/ppq

to contact customer support. You fill out the form and click "Submit," but for a split second, a pop-up appears:

"we`re sorry. There was an error creating your case. Please try again"

and than redirect.

You might try switching browsers, using private/incognito mode, changing devices (desktop, phone), or even using a different IP address—but nothing works. You keep encountering the same error. However, as soon as you change the email address to one not associated with the restricted account, the form submits successfully. This proves, beyond a doubt, that the "error" was linked solely to the email address; changing the email—while keeping everything else the same—changes the outcome.

Okay, so you’ve submitted the request—what happens next? You receive a response (here are some excerpts; the exact wording may vary slightly):

"You are contacting us from an email address that differs from the one registered to your account."

"An account restriction should not, in itself, prevent you from contacting us via the provided form."

"To protect privacy, I cannot, without a direct request from the account owner sent from their registered email address, do the following:"

"Therefore, please reach out to us using the form mentioned above, ensuring you use the email address registered to your account. This will allow us to proceed with reviewing your inquiry and provide the necessary assistance."

Brilliant. In other words, LinkedIn blocks support requests made using the email address linked to a restricted account—yet when they receive a request made (out of necessity) from a different email address, they close the ticket and instruct you to submit a new one using the "correct" email—which is technically impossible to do.
